summary: Defines how to use the ACE framework to give keying material and configuration parameters for secure group communication. Authorized candidate members interact with a Key Distribution Center to get what they need to talk with other group members.

eli5.summary: A club hands out a secret handshake only to approved members. This explains how small devices get approved and receive the group's shared key.

questions: what is an ace key distribution center
how does a device join a group with ace
what is group rekeying in ace
subtitle: How small devices get approved for a secure group and receive the group's keys from a Key Distribution Center.

tldr.problem: Constrained devices that talk as a group need shared keying material, and only authorized devices should get it. Different group protocols need different keys, but the way devices ask for them should not have to be reinvented each time.
tldr.mechanism: A device first gets an access token from the ACE Authorization Server, then presents it to a Key Distribution Center (KDC) that acts as the Resource Server. It then joins through a defined set of KDC resources and receives the group keys, and the KDC rekeys the group as membership changes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9594 fixes the common messages and the KDC interface, and leaves the details of each group protocol to separate application profiles, which must meet listed compliance requirements.

today: RFC 9594 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2024. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This document builds on the Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) framework (RFC 9200). It defines how to request, distribute and renew keying material and configuration parameters that protect messages in a group. A candidate member acts as an ACE Client. A Key Distribution Center (KDC), acting as the ACE Resource Server for the group, gives authorized Clients the keys they need.

The RFC defines the KDC's operations and interface and the general message formats. Communication inside a group can use different approaches, such as multicast or publish-subscribe, protected in different ways. So the details are delegated to separate application profiles, and Appendix A lists the compliance requirements for them. Requirements that profiles are REQUIRED to fulfill have identifiers starting with "REQ", and those they MAY fulfill start with "OPT".

Data is encoded with CBOR (RFC 8949), although JSON is possible through the conversion method in that RFC. The word "group" here means a security group: nodes sharing keying material. It is not the same as an application group or an IP multicast group.

The RFC also explains why rekeying matters. Backward security (new members cannot read earlier traffic) needs a rekey whenever someone joins. Forward security (former members cannot read later traffic) needs a rekey whenever someone leaves or is evicted.
sections.eli5: Lots of small gadgets want to chat in a private group. This paper says how they get the group's secret key, and leaves the kind of chat to other papers.

sections.title: Participants and Overall Flow
sections.content:
Key provisioning has two phases. The first follows the ACE framework between the Client, the Authorization Server (AS) and the KDC. The second is the actual key distribution between the Client and the KDC, which is not based on ACE.

  • Client: a node that wants to join and take part in group communication, possibly with different roles.
  • AS: enforces whether a node may join and with which roles and rights, such as read or write.
  • KDC: keeps the group keying material and gives it to authorized Clients. In the first phase it acts as the ACE Resource Server.
  • Group members: nodes that have joined and protect messages with the group keys.
  • Dispatcher: the entity through which one-to-many messages reach the group, such as a pub-sub Broker, a relayer, or an implicit multicast setting. It does not have the group keying material.

The flow for a joining node is: obtain an access token from the AS, transfer it to the KDC and establish a secure association, send a Join Request to the group-membership resource, keep the association for later key management, and then communicate with the group using the keys obtained at the join.
sections.eli5: You get a pass from the front desk, show it to the key keeper, and get the club's secret. Messengers can carry club notes around but cannot read them.

sections.title: Getting Authorization to Join
sections.content:
The Client sends an Authorization Request to the AS. The AS checks the request and replies with a proof-of-possession access token and parameters for securely talking to the KDC. The Client then sends a Token Transfer Request, a CoAP POST to the /authz-info endpoint of the KDC, and receives a 2.01 (Created) response.

The scope names the groups and optionally the roles the Client wants. By default it is a CBOR byte string wrapping entries in the Authorization Information Format (AIF, RFC 9237), and a textual format is also defined. The access token MUST carry a confirmation claim, an expiration time claim and a scope claim. An extended scope format (Section 7) wraps the scope in a CBOR tag that names its semantics, so a Resource Server with several applications can interpret it.

This exchange differs from plain ACE in two ways. The request MAY carry sign_info set to null, asking for the signature algorithm, its parameters, the key parameters and the credential format used in the groups. The response has a payload, even though ACE defines none there. If a role requires the Client to send its own authentication credential, the response MUST include a kdcchallenge value that the Client later uses in its proof of possession. Transport profiles such as the DTLS or OSCORE profiles (RFC 9202, RFC 9203) secure these exchanges.
sections.eli5: The front desk checks your name and gives you a pass that says which clubs you may enter and what you may do there. The key keeper also gives you a random puzzle to solve later to prove the pass is really yours.

sections.title: The KDC Interface
sections.content:
The KDC exposes a set of resources under a root path. The name ace-group is only a default. Request and success messages that carry a payload MUST use Content-Format application/ace-groupcomm+cbor, with CBOR map keys defined in Section 8.

  • /ace-group: a FETCH with group identifiers returns the matching group names and group-membership URIs.
  • /ace-group/GROUPNAME: the group-membership resource. POST joins the group, and GET returns the current group keying material.
  • /creds: authentication credentials of group members, by GET for all or FETCH with filters.
  • /kdc-cred: the KDC's own authentication credential, if one is required.
  • /policies and /num: the group policies and the version number of the keying material.
  • /nodes/NODENAME: one per member, holding group and individual keying material. GET retrieves it, POST asks for new individual keying material, and DELETE leaves the group.
  • /nodes/NODENAME/cred: POST uploads a new authentication credential.

Application profiles must define which actions are allowed on each resource depending on roles (REQ11), say which resources the KDC does not host (REQ9), and register a Resource Type for the group-membership resources (REQ10).
sections.eli5: The key keeper's office has labelled drawers: one for the member list, one for the current secret, one for each member's own notes. What you may open depends on your pass.

sections.title: Joining and Leaving
sections.content:
In the Join Request (a POST to the group-membership resource) the Client can include scope, get_creds, client_cred, cnonce, client_cred_verify, creds_repo and control_uri. The cnonce is required. If the Client sends its own credential, the client_cred_verify value is proof-of-possession evidence computed over the scope, the KDC's challenge N_S and the Client's nonce N_C. A typical form is a signature made with the private key matching the credential.

The KDC checks that the token covers the requested roles, otherwise replying 4.03 (Forbidden). It checks the credential for the group, replying 4.00 (Bad Request) with error id 2 on a mismatch, and verifies the proof, replying 4.00 with error id 3 on failure. If the stored kdcchallenge is gone, it sends a fresh one in a 4.00 response.

On success the KDC adds the Client to the group, creates /ace-group/GROUPNAME/nodes/NODENAME, and may rekey if backward security is required. The Join Response is 2.01 (Created), or 2.04 (Changed) for a rejoin. It MUST carry gkty, key and num (a strictly increasing version number), and SHOULD carry exp and exi for the lifetime of the keys. If the Client does not know UTC, it relies on exi. Optional fields include creds, peer_roles and ace_groupcomm_profile.

A Client leaves with a DELETE on its node resource. It can rejoin without a new token while its access token is still valid. The KDC can also evict a member that is compromised or whose authorization has expired or been revoked. In every removal the KDC deletes the member's challenge and sub-resource, and it MAY tell an evicted member through the control_uri or an unsolicited 4.04 (Not Found) with error id 5.
sections.eli5: To join, you hand over your pass and prove it is yours, and the key keeper hands you the secret and a version number. To leave, you tell the keeper, who crosses you off the list.

sections.title: Group Rekeying
sections.content:
A group rekeying is started and driven only by the KDC. Members cannot ask for one. Reasons include a membership change, keys nearing expiration, or a regular schedule. The KDC MUST increment the version number NUM before distributing the new keys as NUM+1, and once done it MUST delete the old keys.

Each rekeying message uses Content-Format application/ace-groupcomm+cbor and carries at least gkty, key and num. The KDC MUST support at least the basic Point-to-Point scheme (rekeying_scheme value 0), where it sends one protected message to each target member. It SHOULD make the group-membership resource observable (CoAP Observe, RFC 7641) and can also POST to a member's control_uri. A member that did none of these cannot take part and has to fetch the keys with a GET after repeated failures.

The RFC also gives recommendations for one-to-many schemes such as those in RFC 2093, RFC 2094 and RFC 2627. They usually need fewer messages, which pays off in large groups, but need extra administrative keying material and signatures on rekeying messages.

Rekeying can briefly leave members with mismatched keys. A receiver may get a message under the old keys after it has the new ones, or the reverse. Retaining old keys for a limited time helps the first case, but a former compromised member could exploit it, so conservative policy does not keep old keys. In the second case the receiver should ask the KDC for the latest keys, for example after several decryption failures.
sections.eli5: When someone leaves the club, the keeper invents a new secret handshake and tells everyone who is still in. If a friend has not heard yet, they can ask the keeper.

sections.title: Errors and Problem Details
sections.content:
The KDC MUST reply 4.01 (Unauthorized) if it has no valid access token for the Client. If the token lacks a scope entry for the group, or its roles do not allow the operation, the KDC replies 4.03 (Forbidden). Badly formed requests get 4.00 (Bad Request), and unknown fields MUST be silently ignored.

Some errors use the Concise Problem Details format (RFC 9290) with Content-Format application/concise-problem-details+cbor. It MUST include a custom entry ace-groupcomm-error holding an error-id integer. Clients are not required to support this format, but a Client that understands an identifier can use it to decide what to do next, for example waiting and retrying after error 4.
sections.eli5: When the keeper says no, they also hand over a small card with a number saying why, so you know whether to wait, fix your pass, or start over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations are inherited from the ACE framework (RFC 9200) and from the transport profile in use. The KDC is trusted a great deal, because it generates and provides the symmetric group keys and can decrypt group traffic protected with commonly shared keys. A compromised KDC could therefore control and rekey the group, take part in it without authorization, let others do so, and build wrong links between node identifiers and credentials. If the group protocol uses source authentication such as signatures, the KDC still cannot impersonate members because it lacks their private keys.

Receivers need a mechanism against replayed messages and to check freshness, for example the ones cited from RFC 8613 and Group OSCORE. The KDC SHOULD renew keys on a membership change unless a profile says otherwise. It SHOULD give even a client joining an empty group keys never used before in that group. It may rekey less often if joins and leaves are frequent, but then backward and forward security are not constantly preserved, which is typically undesirable for a leaving member who is suspected to be compromised. The KDC also needs to detect nodes that repeatedly trigger rekeying, such as by leaving and rejoining at high rates, and needs congestion control when it distributes new keys. Section 10.3 notes that changing keys during a Block-Wise transfer may cost extra bandwidth for resent blocks.
sections.eli5: The key keeper knows the secret, so everyone must trust them. And if the secret is not changed when members come and go, old members or newcomers might hear things they should not.
